title: ECCO: Evidence-Driven Causal Reasoning for Compiler Optimization
claim: Choosing and ordering optimization steps is a vast combinatorial search, and fixed heuristics and black-box learned tuners both fall short.
layout: 3 stacked sections: task, challenge maze, then two contrasting approaches side by side
description: The figure has three parts. The top box, "The Core Task: Compiler Phase Ordering", pairs a short definition with a row of pass blocks (Pass A to E) on a pipeline bar, with bypass arrows showing reordering, ending in "Optimized Code". The middle box, "The Challenge: A Massive Search Space", shows an isometric gray maze with peaks and an "Optimal Solution" flag, to convey a non-convex combinatorial landscape. The bottom is split by a vertical divider. On the left, "Fixed Heuristics" shows a locked sequence of Pass 1 to N (e.g. -O3) that gives suboptimal results. On the right, "Auto-Tuning with Machine Learning" shows a cycle of Pass X, Y and Z around a brain labeled ML/RL, with a performance-metric feedback loop and a "Limitation" box about black-box behavior. The blocks are slate blue, green and gray. The eye goes first to the maze.
caption: Overview of the compiler phase-ordering task.
abstract: Compiler auto-tuning faces a dichotomy between traditional black-box search methods, which lack semantic guidance, and recent Large Language Model (LLM) approaches, which often suffer from superficial pattern matching and causal opacity. In this paper, we introduce ECCO, a framework that bridges interpretable reasoning with combinatorial search. We first propose a reverse engineering methodology to construct a Chain-of-Thought dataset, explicitly mapping static code features to verifiable performance evidence. This enables the model to learn the causal logic governing optimization decisions rather than merely imitating sequences. Leveraging this interpretable prior, we design a collaborative inference mechanism where the LLM functions as a strategist, defining optimization intents that dynamically guide the mutation operations of a genetic algorithm. Experimental results on seven datasets demonstrate that ECCO significantly outperforms the LLVM opt -O3 baseline, achieving an average 24.44% reduction in cycles.
